faqs.question: What is a rational equation, and how is it different from a rational expression?
faqs.answer: A rational expression is a ratio of two polynomials, like \( \dfrac{x-3}{x-8} \) — it has no equals sign, so there's nothing to solve, only something to simplify or evaluate. A rational equation sets two such expressions (or a mix of expressions and constants) equal to each other, like \( \dfrac{2}{x+5}=\dfrac{x-3}{x-8}-7 \) — now there's a specific value (or values) of x that makes the whole statement true, and finding it is the actual task.

faqs.question: Why do I need to find excluded values before I even start solving?
faqs.answer:
Because whatever value makes a denominator equal to zero can never be part of the solution — division by zero is undefined, full stop, no matter what the rest of the equation looks like. Finding these values up front means you already know, before you do a single step of algebra, which answers you'll have to reject later if they show up.

The same four steps solve every rational equation in this section — step 1 and step 4 are what keep you from accepting an invalid answer.

faqs.question: Why can solving a rational equation produce a "solution" that isn't actually valid?
faqs.answer: The step that clears the fractions (multiplying every term by the LCD) is a legitimate algebra move, but it also creates a brand new equation — one with no denominators left at all, which no longer \"remembers\" that certain values were off-limits in the original. That cleared equation can therefore hand you back exactly one of those forbidden values as an answer, since nothing in its own structure forbids it anymore. Checking every candidate against your excluded-values list (faq-2) is what catches this.

faqs.question: When can I use cross-multiplication, and how does it relate to clearing denominators in general?
faqs.answer:
Cross-multiplication works specifically when the equation is in the form \( \dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{c}{d} \) — a single fraction equal to a single fraction, nothing else added or subtracted on either side. It isn't actually a separate technique: multiplying both sides by \( b \) and by \( d \) (the general 'clear the fractions' method) produces exactly the same equation, \( ad=bc \), that cross-multiplying gives you directly. It's a shortcut for one specific, common equation shape, not a new rule.
Worked Example

\( \dfrac{4}{x+1}=-\dfrac{2}{x+6} \) is in exactly this form, so cross-multiplying gives \( 4(x+6)=-2(x+1) \) immediately.

faqs.question: How do I find the values that must be excluded from a rational equation's solutions?
faqs.answer:
Set every distinct denominator in the equation equal to zero and solve each one — every value you get has to be excluded, since it would make some part of the original equation undefined.
Worked Example

For \( \dfrac{2x}{x-1}-\dfrac{3}{x-3}=\dfrac{x^2-11x+18}{x^2-4x+3} \): the denominators are \( x-1 \), \( x-3 \), and \( x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3) \) — all pointing to the same two excluded values, \( x=1 \) and \( x=3 \).

faqs.question: How do I clear fractions when there's a constant term in the equation, not just another fraction?
faqs.answer:
Multiply every single term by the LCD — including any bare constant, not only the fractions. Skipping a term because it "doesn't have a denominator" is a common way to get the wrong cleared equation.
Worked Example

\( 5=-\dfrac{6}{x-2} \): multiply both terms by \( x-2 \): \( 5(x-2)=-6 \), which solves to \( x=\dfrac{4}{5} \) (and \( \tfrac{4}{5}\neq 2 \), so it's valid).

faqs.question: How do I clear fractions when the denominators aren't already the same or simply related?
faqs.answer:
Multiply every term by the full LCD — the product of every distinct denominator that appears, unless some of them share common factors, in which case use the smallest expression that still contains every denominator as a factor.
Worked Example

\( \dfrac{x}{x+2}=-\dfrac{2}{x+2}-\dfrac{2}{5} \): the LCD is \( 5(x+2) \). Multiplying every term by it gives \( 5x=-10-2(x+2) \), with no fractions left.

faqs.question: How do I solve a rational equation that simplifies to a quadratic equation?
faqs.answer:
Clear the fractions as usual, and if the result is a quadratic rather than a linear equation, solve it exactly like any other quadratic — factor it, or use the quadratic formula — and then check every candidate root against your excluded values.
Worked Example

\( \dfrac{2x}{x-1}-\dfrac{3}{x-3}=\dfrac{x^2-11x+18}{x^2-4x+3} \), excluded values \( x=1,3 \) (faq-5): clearing fractions gives \( 2x(x-3)-3(x-1)=x^2-11x+18 \), which simplifies to \( x^2+2x-15=0 \).

Factoring: \( (x+5)(x-3)=0 \), so the candidates are \( x=-5 \) and \( x=3 \).

Since \( x=3 \) is excluded, only \( x=-5 \) is a valid solution.

faqs.question: How do I check whether a candidate solution is actually valid?
faqs.answer:
Compare it against your excluded-values list from faq-5 — if it matches one of those values, reject it immediately, no further work needed. If it doesn't match, you can also plug it back into the ORIGINAL equation (with the fractions still in place) as a final confirmation that everything checks out.

For x/(x+2) = −2/(x+2) − 2/5, clearing fractions gives the candidate x = −2 — but x = −2 is exactly the value excluded in step 1. The candidate and the excluded value land on the same point, so it isn't a real solution.

faqs.question: What does it mean when every candidate solution turns out to be excluded?
faqs.answer: It means the rational equation genuinely has NO SOLUTION — not that you made a mistake somewhere. This is a completely valid, correct final answer in its own right, and it's exactly why checking candidates against the excluded list (rather than skipping that step) matters: without it, you'd have wrongly reported an invalid value as if it were a real answer.

faqs.question: How does finding excluded values here connect to domain restrictions in general?
faqs.answer: An excluded value in a rational equation is exactly the same idea as a restricted value in a rational function's domain — both come from asking \"where does a denominator equal zero?\" The only difference is what you do with that information afterward: for a function, it tells you where the domain stops; for an equation, it tells you which candidate answers must be thrown out.

faqs.question: How does this connect to PR7's rational function graphs (vertical asymptotes and holes)?
faqs.answer: The excluded values you find here are precisely the x-values where PR7's rational functions have a vertical asymptote or a hole — the graph simply cannot exist at those points. An extraneous \"solution\" (faq-3, faq-10) is really just an algebra process momentarily forgetting that the function was never defined there in the first place; PR7 makes visible, on a graph, exactly the restriction this section enforces symbolically.

faqs.question: Why do rational equations matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Rational equations show up anywhere a rate, a ratio, or a combined process is involved — mixing solutions of different concentrations, combined work rates (two people or machines working together), or resistors wired in parallel in a circuit all lead directly to a rational equation. Recognizing which values are physically impossible to begin with (like a negative amount of time, or a resistance of zero) is often the real-world version of checking for excluded values.

guided.title: Practice Finding Excluded Values
guided.prompt: I'm learning to find excluded values before solving a rational equation. Give me a rational equation and ask me to identify every value that must be excluded, by setting each denominator equal to zero. Give me a few more examples of increasing difficulty, including one where two different denominators share a common factor.

guided.title: Practice Clearing Fractions
guided.prompt: Give me a rational equation and walk me through clearing the fractions: finding the LCD, multiplying every term by it, and simplifying. Include at least one example with a constant term (not just fractions) so I practice remembering to multiply that term too.

guided.title: Practice Solving and Checking Candidates
guided.prompt: Give me a rational equation that simplifies into a quadratic after clearing fractions. Walk me through finding the excluded values first, then clearing fractions, solving the quadratic, and checking each candidate solution against the excluded list. Make sure at least one problem has a candidate that gets thrown out.

guided.title: Recognize When There's No Solution
guided.prompt: Give me a rational equation where every candidate solution turns out to be excluded, so the final answer is 'no solution.' Walk me through the whole process so I can see exactly where and why this happens, and help me understand why this is a valid final answer rather than a mistake.

guided.title: Connect Excluded Values to Rational Function Graphs
guided.prompt: I've learned to find excluded values when solving rational equations, and I know this connects to vertical asymptotes and holes in rational function graphs (PR7). Can you help me see this connection with a specific example — show me a rational equation and its matching rational function, and point out exactly how the excluded value shows up in both places?
